newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russians protest from Pacific to Baltic over wages.
newsitem.headline: Russians protest from Pacific to Baltic over wages.

text.p: At least 1.8 million Russians, some waving communist red flags and singing socialist songs, protested in cities from the Pacific Ocean to the Baltic Sea on Thursday against unpaid wages and government policy.

But 11th-hour efforts by the Kremlin to ease tensions appeared to pay off. The number of protesters fell short of the expectations of the trade union organisers in the nuclear state of 150 million people and there were no reports of violence.

The Interior Ministry was quoted by Interfax news agency as saying 1.8 million people had taken part in about 1,300 protests across Russia -- about one tenth of that forecast by the trade unions, who did not release a final figure.

The biggest protests were staged in a sunny, frosty Moscow where police put the number of demonstrators at over 80,000 and in St Petersburg, where 40,000 people in the central Palace Square had to contend with heavy snow.
St Petersburg radio said factories started paying wage arrears at 3 p.m. (1200 GMT), just when the speeches started.

The unions, backed by Russia's communist-led opposition, organised the strikes and demonstrations to protest at wage arrears of more than 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion), including 10 trillion from the state.
Millions of workers have not been paid for months and cannot afford the goods now crowding the shelves of once-empty shops.
"Tens of millions of people have been reduced to poverty," Alexander Lebed, one of President Boris Yeltsin's most outspoken opponents, told NTV commercial television.

"One gets the impression that it has been decided that a third of the population of the country are to be killed off. We have to let off steam," he said. "Neither the president nor government is in control of the situation in the country."

Slogans demanding the resignation of Yeltsin and the government of Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin floated high above many of the crowds, accompanied by red flags and portraits of Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov told reporters the protest amounted to a no-confidence vote in the cabinet, despite a reshuffle which was completed on Wednesday.
"Changes in the government have convinced no one. This march is going from (the Pacific city of) Vladivostok to Kaliningrad (on the Baltic) and no one can stop it," he told reporters.
But the dominant mood was mostly resigned. In Vladivostok, 7,000 km (4,500 miles) east of Moscow, brass bands played and the crowd of at least 15,000 sang socialist songs.
In St Petersburg, where protests started many hours later on the opposite side of Russia, one man carried a skeleton with a banner saying: "This used to be a biology teacher."
Thousands of police were placed on alert but no major violence or clashes were reported.
The government's last-minute efforts to quell popular discontent appeared to have partial success.

Chernomyrdin promised on Wednesday that the state and private employers would pay 11.8 trillion roubles ($2 billion) in back wages and pensions in March. It was not clear where the money would come from.
Billions of roubles have been dispatched hastily to regions and working groups ahead of the protest.

A Kremlin spokesman said Yeltsin, 66, was following the action from a country residence and considered economic demands by the protesters "justified". He has blamed the government for the huge backlog in wages.
The protests are the first test for Russia's new reformist-looking cabinet, which has been named gradually over recent weeks and vowed to resolve the crisis quickly.
"I want to live without shocks and without Yeltsin's therapy," read one banner in Vladivostok, referring to market reforms which were launched in 1992 but have largely stalled.

The protests were far from universal. Most miners, a group hit hard by pay arrears, did not strike and said they were not calling on Yeltsin's government to quit. They have decided to give the new government a chance.
